title: Sebastian and the Inventory
premise: Edmund Iversen, a night librarian drifting through a sleepless city, attends the funeral of his estranged uncle Sebastian and is approached by a stranger who calls the family by their old name — Ivarsen — a name buried decades ago. The stranger leaves behind a ledger from Sebastian's private 'inventory': a record of wrongs committed by the city's most powerful developer, Halvard Voss, whose new tower will soon demolish the house where it all began. As Edmund investigates the inventory's entries, he discovers his family's complicity in a cover-up that ruined an innocent man, and must choose between protecting the last shreds of his family's reputation and exposing the truth. In the end, Edmund testifies at the demolition hearing, the house falls anyway, but Voss's empire cracks under the light of day — and Edmund finally stops being a tenant of his own life.
about_author: C. M. Reyes is the pen name of a former municipal archivist who spent eleven years cataloguing property disputes and probate files before turning to fiction. They write quietly devastating novels about ordinary people caught in the machinery of institutions.

chapters.title: The Hours After Closing
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. We meet him shelving books at 3 a.m., invisible in a city that never sleeps, estranged from a family he sees once a year. A letter arrives: Uncle Sebastian has died. Emotional beat: numb routine cracked open by obligation.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. At the sparse funeral, a gaunt stranger approaches, calls the family 'Ivarsen,' and presses a brass key into Edmund's hand before vanishing. His mother flinches at the old name and refuses to explain. Beat: unease; the past has teeth.

chapters.title: The Key to Number Nine
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. He tracks the key to Sebastian's condemned house on Verlaine Street, slated for demolition in six weeks to make way for Voss Tower. Inside, dust, sealed rooms, and a locked cabinet labeled INVENTORY. Beat: dread mixed with curiosity.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Counts
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. The cabinet holds a ledger: dates, names, sums — payments made and favors owed, all pointing toward developer Halvard Voss. The final entry is unfinished. Beat: the thrill of discovery shadowed by fear of what it implicates.

chapters.title: My Mother's Silence
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Edmund and his mother, Ruth. He confronts her; she admits only that the family changed its name 'for reasons that kept us fed.' She begs him to burn the ledger. Beat: loyalty demanded as a condition of love.

chapters.title: The Stranger Returns
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. The stranger — Tomas Reyes, no relation to the author — reveals himself as the son of Aurelio Cruz, the man the Ivarsens helped destroy thirty years ago. He wants the ledger for a hearing that could stop the demolition. Beat: alliance offered, motives unclear.

chapters.title: Entries One Through Seven
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, interwoven with ledger excerpts. Each entry maps a small corruption: bribed inspectors, silenced tenants, a fire ruled accidental. Edmund recognizes his father's handwriting beside Sebastian's. Beat: the family myth collapses entry by entry.

chapters.title: Voss
chapters.summary: Voss's POV. The developer learns someone has been inside the Verlaine Street house. Charming, ruthless, genuinely convinced he built the city's future, he orders the demolition date moved up. Beat: power shown as self-justifying certainty.

chapters.title: The Tenant Below
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. He finds the last holdout tenant of Verlaine Street, elderly Mrs. Okafor, who remembers Aurelio Cruz and the night of the fire. Her testimony fills the ledger's gaps. Beat: grief transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: What Father Knew
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV, flashback structure. She recalls her husband's guilt, his late-night calls with Sebastian, and the payment that bought the family's silence after the fire. Beat: complicity examined from inside; shame inherited like furniture.

chapters.title: An Offer, Politely Made
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Voss invites Edmund to lunch, offers money for the ledger and a job 'worthy of your talents.' Edmund declines — then finds his library job eliminated within the week. Beat: power's velvet threat; the cost of refusal begins.

chapters.title: The Missing Page
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The ledger's eighth page — naming who actually set the fire — is torn out. Suspicion falls on everyone; Tomas accuses Edmund's family of destroying it. Their fragile alliance fractures. Beat: truth weaponized against trust.

chapters.title: Sebastian's Room
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Searching the sealed upstairs room, Edmund finds his uncle's letters and a photograph: Sebastian and Aurelio Cruz as young friends. Sebastian wasn't just recording sins — he was trying to atone. Beat: the dead uncle becomes human.

chapters.title: Pressure
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Voss's lawyers file a nuisance suit; Mrs. Okafor receives a buyout she can't refuse; Ruth stops answering Edmund's calls. The walls close in from every direction. Beat: isolation engineered by institutional power.

chapters.title: The Confession Tape
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Among Sebastian's effects, a cassette: Sebastian interviewing his dying brother — Edmund's father — who admits the fire was set to drive out Cruz, and names the torn page's keeper. Beat: horror and terrible relief; truth survives in unexpected vessels.

chapters.title: Ruth's Choice
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Confronted with the tape, Ruth must decide between burying her husband's crime forever or letting her son hand it to the world. She chooses, at last, to stand beside him. Beat: loyalty redefined — not protection from truth, but solidarity within it.

chapters.title: Breaking Into the Record Room
chapters.summary: Edmund and Tomas's POV, alternating. The torn page sits in a sealed probate archive; they break in the night before the hearing, recovering the page that names Voss himself as the one who lit the match. Beat: justice pursued outside the law, hearts pounding.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. At the demolition and land-use hearing, Edmund presents the ledger, the tape, and the page. Voss's lawyers counter brilliantly; the room turns against Edmund until Mrs. Okafor rises to speak. Beat: climax — one voice against the machine.

chapters.title: What Falls
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The demolition proceeds — the house comes down regardless — but the evidence leaks to a journalist, and investigations into Voss begin. Victory and loss arrive in the same breath. Beat: bitterswet catharsis; truth costs more than it pays.

chapters.title: Reckonings
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Voss resigns under investigation; Tomas reconciles with Edmund over what remains of Aurelio's life; Ruth visits the rubble and leaves flowers. Old debts acknowledged, if not repaid. Beat: quiet accountability, imperfect peace.

chapters.title: The New Inventory
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. He begins his own ledger — not of wrongs but of truths owed: names, debts, promises. He takes a job archiving the city's condemned buildings so their stories outlast the wrecking ball. Beat: purpose found in witness.

chapters.title: Owner of His Hours
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, closing chapter. A year later, Edmund walks the city at dawn, no longer a tenant of his own life. He passes the finished base of Voss Tower, stalled mid-construction, and feels the weight of the ledger in his bag like a heartbeat. Beat: resolution — belonging earned through truth.
